#### About Immanuel Kant

Immanuel Kant (1724–1804) spent nearly his entire life in Königsberg, rising from tutor to professor at the university there. After early scientific and metaphysical essays, the Critique of Pure Reason (1781/1787) launched his “critical” philosophy.

### Interpretation

This is the formula Kant calls the categorical imperative: act only on a maxim you could will as a universal law. The test is not whether you would like the consequences but whether the rule you are acting on can be stated without contradiction when universalised. A maxim fails if willing it universally would destroy what the action is for — as a lying promise would destroy the trust that makes promising work. The criterion is thus logical, not consequentialist.

#### Why it matters

Its practical use is as a consistency check: state the rule you are about to act on, then ask what happens if everyone follows it. Many excuses do not survive being written down.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “Act so that the maxim of your will…”?

“Act so that the maxim of your will…” comes from Kritik der praktischen Vernunft (1788), attributed to Immanuel Kant.

#### What does Immanuel Kant mean by morality?

Moral philosophy asks whether morality is objective, how reasons bind us, and how character, rules, and consequences relate. Traditions differ on whether duty, virtue, or outcomes come first. This passage enters that discussion through morality.
